claim: IgM-BCR activation is dependent on mechanical forces.
source: We observed that IgM-BCR activation is dependent on mechanical forces and exhibits a multi-threshold effect.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that different mechanical force levels (12-56 pN) produce different levels of IgM-BCR activation, as measured by BCR accumulation and signaling molecule recruitment.

claim: IgM-BCR activation exhibits a multi-threshold effect.
source: We observed that IgM-BCR activation is dependent on mechanical forces and exhibits a multi-threshold effect.
evidence: Data in Figures 2 and 3 show three distinct threshold levels: low-force (12-16 pN), medium-force (23-43 pN), and high-force (50-56 pN) NP-TGT sensors triggering weak, medium, and strong activation respectively.

claim: The activation of isotype-switched IgG-BCR only requires a low threshold of less than 12 pN.
source: In contrast, the activation of isotype-switched IgG- or IgE-BCR only requires a low threshold of less than 12 pN, providing an explanation for their rapid activation in response to antigen stimulation.
evidence: Figure 6 shows that 12 pN, 43 pN, and 56 pN NP-TGT sensors all similarly activate IgG-BCR, indicating the threshold is below 12 pN.

claim: The activation of isotype-switched IgE-BCR only requires a low threshold of less than 12 pN.
source: In contrast, the activation of isotype-switched IgG- or IgE-BCR only requires a low threshold of less than 12 pN, providing an explanation for their rapid activation in response to antigen stimulation.
evidence: Figure 6I,J shows that IgE-BCR activation is similar across different force levels (12-56 pN), indicating a threshold below 12 pN.

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of the IgG-BCR heavy chain is both required and sufficient to account for the low mechanical force threshold.
source: Mechanistically, we found that the cytoplasmic tail of the IgG-BCR heavy chain is both required and sufficient to account for the low mechanical force threshold.
evidence: Figure 7 shows that swapping the cytoplasmic tail of IgM with IgG tail (MMG) results in force-independent activation, while swapping IgG tail with IgM tail (GGM) results in force-dependent activation.

claim: B lymphocytes use B cell receptors (BCRs) to sense the physical features of antigens.
source: B lymphocytes use B cell receptors (BCRs) to sense the physical features of the antigens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The BCR is composed of a membrane-bound immunoglobulin (mIg) and a non-covalently associated heterodimer of Igα and Igβ in a 1 mIg: 1 Igα–Igβ heterodimer stoichiometry.
source: The BCR is composed of a membrane-bound immunoglobulin (mIg) and a non-covalently associated heterodimer of Igα and Igβ in a 1 mIg: 1 Igα–Igβ heterodimer stoichiometry (Schamel and Reth, 2000; Tolar et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Schamel and Reth (2000) and Tolar et al. (2005).

claim: BCR activation is efficiently regulated by antigen density.
source: These forms include antigen density (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen affinity (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen valency (Bachmann et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2004; Liu and Chen, 2005), the Brownian mobility feature of the antigen (Wan and Liu, 2012), and the stiffness feature of the substrates presenting the antigen (Wan et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fleire et al., 2006 and Liu et al., 2010a.

claim: BCR activation is efficiently regulated by antigen affinity.
source: These forms include antigen density (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen affinity (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen valency (Bachmann et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2004; Liu and Chen, 2005), the Brownian mobility feature of the antigen (Wan and Liu, 2012), and the stiffness feature of the substrates presenting the antigen (Wan et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fleire et al., 2006 and Liu et al., 2010a.

claim: BCR activation is efficiently regulated by antigen valency.
source: These forms include antigen density (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen affinity (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen valency (Bachmann et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2004; Liu and Chen, 2005), the Brownian mobility feature of the antigen (Wan and Liu, 2012), and the stiffness feature of the substrates presenting the antigen (Wan et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bachmann et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2004; and Liu and Chen, 2005.

claim: BCR activation is efficiently regulated by the Brownian mobility feature of the antigen.
source: These forms include antigen density (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen affinity (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen valency (Bachmann et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2004; Liu and Chen, 2005), the Brownian mobility feature of the antigen (Wan and Liu, 2012), and the stiffness feature of the substrates presenting the antigen (Wan et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wan and Liu, 2012.

claim: BCR activation is efficiently regulated by the stiffness feature of the substrates presenting the antigen.
source: These forms include antigen density (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen affinity (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a), antigen valency (Bachmann et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2004; Liu and Chen, 2005), the Brownian mobility feature of the antigen (Wan and Liu, 2012), and the stiffness feature of the substrates presenting the antigen (Wan et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wan et al., 2013 and Zeng et al., 2015.

claim: B cells use mechanical forces to rupture the bonds between BCRs and membrane-bound antigens.
source: For example, a recent study by Tolar and his colleagues demonstrated that B cells used the mechanical forces to rupture the bonds between BCRs and membrane-bound antigens.
evidence: This claim is attributed to a study by Tolar and colleagues, as indicated by the citation context.

claim: Only high affinity BCR and antigen microclusters are internalized for antigen processing.
source: The authors found that only the high affinity BCR and antigen microclusters would be internalized for antigen processing, giving a new mechanism to explain B cell affinity discrimination (Natkanski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Natkanski et al., 2013.

claim: Viral capsid substrates presenting antigen exhibit a high degree of stiffness (45,000–1,000,000 kPa).
source: For example, viral capsid substrates presenting antigen exhibited a high degree of stiffness (45,000–1,000,000 kPa) (Mateu, 2012), while substrates presenting antigen on the membrane of the host cell infected by virus showed a medium level of stiffness (0.01–1000 kPa) (Nemir and West, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mateu, 2012.

claim: Substrates presenting antigen on the membrane of host cells infected by virus show a medium level of stiffness (0.01–1000 kPa).
source: For example, viral capsid substrates presenting antigen exhibited a high degree of stiffness (45,000–1,000,000 kPa) (Mateu, 2012), while substrates presenting antigen on the membrane of the host cell infected by virus showed a medium level of stiffness (0.01–1000 kPa) (Nemir and West, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nemir and West, 2010.

claim: Extracellular matrix (ECM) exhibits a range of stiffness from 0.012 to 20 kPa.
source: Additionally, B cells can also efficiently acquire antigens that are associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) in the tissue (Ciechomska et al., 2014), which is well documented to exhibit an extraordinary range of stiffness from 0.012 to 20 kPa (Bao and Suresh, 2003; Engler et al., 2004; Paszek et al., 2005; Nemir and West, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bao and Suresh, 2003; Engler et al., 2004; Paszek et al., 2005; and Nemir and West, 2010.

claim: Soluble antigen in plasma displays a remarkably low level of stiffness (several Pa).
source: Soluble antigen in plasma has also been detected and displayed a remarkably low level of stiffness (several Pa) (Araujo Gde et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Araujo Gde et al., 2012.

claim: The NP-TGT system has the same tension gauge scales as the original TGT system developed by Ha and colleagues.
source: Since we just exchanged the cyclic RGDfk peptide with the NP hapten antigen and did not change the sequence and design of these dsDNA-based TGT sensors, our NP-TGT system shall have the same tension gauge scales as the one used by Ha and his colleagues (Wang and Ha, 2013).
evidence: The authors state they only changed the ligand (from RGDfk to NP) but kept the DNA design identical, thus maintaining the same force calibration.

claim: The specific force value of each dsDNA-based mechanical force sensor presents a distribution with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 5 pN for unzipping rupture mode and 15 pN for shearing rupture mode.
source: A key feature of dsDNA-based mechanical force sensor is that the specific force value of each sensor is not an absolute value but presents a distribution with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 5 pN for unzipping rupture mode and 15 pN for shearing rupture mode (Lang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lang et al., 2004.

claim: J558L cells expressing B1-8-IgM-BCR initiate activation responses when encountering 56 pN NP-TGT sensor.
source: We found that J558L cells expressing B1-8-IgM-BCR initiated the activation responses as quantified by the dramatic accumulation of BCRs into the contact interface of B cells with coverslip presenting 56 pN NP-TGT sensor and formed a typical B cell immunological synapse (IS) as illustrated by the time lapse TIRFM images (Figure 1C,D, Video 1).
evidence: Figure 1C,D and Video 1 show time-lapse TIRFM images demonstrating BCR accumulation and IS formation.

claim: J558L cells expressing B1-8-IgM-BCR do not initiate activation responses when encountering control TGT without NP conjugation.
source: These results were not observed with the negative control (NC) 56 pN TGT without NP conjugation (Figure 1C,D, Video 1).
evidence: Figure 1C,D and Video 1 show minimal BCR accumulation with control TGT lacking NP antigen.

claim: Neutravidin does not dissociate from the coverslip during a 10-min time course.
source: Additional experiments showed that neutravidin would not dissociate from the coverslip during the 10-min time course of our experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C)
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C shows no significant change in neutravidin fluorescence over 10 minutes.

claim: NP-TGT can only be attached to coverslip in a neutravidin-dependent manner.
source: and NP-TGT can only be attached to coverslip in a neutravidin-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1D shows that NP-TGT attachment requires neutravidin coating.

claim: Non-specific attachment of NP-TGT molecules on coverslip without pre-coated neutravidin cannot induce synaptic accumulation of BCRs.
source: Further experiments also indicated that the non-specific attachment of NP-TGT molecules if any on the coverslip without pre-coated neutravidin cannot induce the synaptic accumulation of BCRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1E shows no BCR accumulation on coverslips lacking neutravidin coating.

claim: Primary mature naive B cells from wild-type C57BL/6 mice do not accumulate BCRs in response to NP-TGT sensor.
source: These primary B cells did not accumulate BCRs into the B cell IS in response to coverslip presenting NP-TGT sensor compared to the case of coverslip alone, although a dramatic accumulation was readily observed in the case of encountering coverslip that was coated with anti-mouse IgM surrogate antigens as a positive control (Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1E shows that wild-type B cells (non-NP-specific) do not respond to NP-TGT but do respond to anti-IgM.

claim: NP-TGT sensors with higher mechanical force trigger more aggressive spreading response and enhanced BCR synaptic accumulation than NP-TGT molecules with lower mechanical force.
source: The results suggested that NP-TGT sensors with higher mechanical force generally triggered more aggressive spreading response and enhanced BCR synaptic accumulation than NP-TGT molecules with lower mechanical force (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Figure 2A-C shows quantification of BCR accumulation and spreading in response to different force levels.

claim: Low-force (12–16 pN) NP-TGT sensors trigger weak activation of IgM-BCR.
source: The low-force (12–16 pN) NP-TGT sensors triggered a weak activation, whereas the middle-force (23–43 pN) NP-TGT sensors initiated a medium-level activation, and the high-force (50–56 pN) NP-TGT sensors accounted for a strong activation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows quantitative data demonstrating three distinct levels of BCR activation corresponding to three force ranges.

claim: Middle-force (23–43 pN) NP-TGT sensors initiate medium-level activation of IgM-BCR.
source: The low-force (12–16 pN) NP-TGT sensors triggered a weak activation, whereas the middle-force (23–43 pN) NP-TGT sensors initiated a medium-level activation, and the high-force (50–56 pN) NP-TGT sensors accounted for a strong activation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows quantitative data demonstrating three distinct levels of BCR activation corresponding to three force ranges.

claim: High-force (50–56 pN) NP-TGT sensors account for strong activation of IgM-BCR.
source: The low-force (12–16 pN) NP-TGT sensors triggered a weak activation, whereas the middle-force (23–43 pN) NP-TGT sensors initiated a medium-level activation, and the high-force (50–56 pN) NP-TGT sensors accounted for a strong activation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows quantitative data demonstrating three distinct levels of BCR activation corresponding to three force ranges.

claim: Increasing mechanical force within a threshold barrier does not result in dramatically enhanced activation responses of IgM-BCRs.
source: However, within these three threshold barriers, increasing the mechanical force, such as from 23 pN to 33 pN or to 43 pN (the medium level threshold), will not result in dramatically enhanced activation responses of IgM-BCRs.
evidence: Figure 2A,B shows that BCR accumulation is similar for 23, 33, and 43 pN sensors, indicating no dramatic increase within this range.

claim: There is no obvious internalization of BCR and antigen molecules during the 10-min time course of the experiments.
source: Using these NP-TGT molecules, we also showed that there were no obvious internalization during the 10-min time course of our experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C), consistent with the published studies (Fleire et al., 2006; Natkanski et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C shows confocal imaging data demonstrating lack of internalization over 10 minutes, consistent with cited literature.

claim: B cells pretreated with MDC inhibitor exhibit dependence on mechanical forces in the synaptic accumulation of IgM-BCRs.
source: Indeed, B cells that were pretreated with monodansylcadaverine (MDC), an inhibitor to block B cell internalization (Tolar et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2010a), also exhibited the dependent on mechanical forces in the synaptic accumulation of the IgM-BCRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2D-F shows that blocking internalization does not eliminate force-dependent BCR accumulation.

claim: The volume of BCR microclusters is dependent on the strength of mechanical force.
source: We similarly observed that the volume of the BCR microclusters is dependent on the strength of the mechanical force with 56 pN NP-TGT sensors producing much bigger and brighter BCR microclusters than 43 pN and 12 pN NP-TGT molecules (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Figure 3A,B shows quantification of BCR microcluster fluorescence intensity at different force levels.

claim: The membrane proximal recruitment of pSyk is dependent on mechanical forces.
source: We found that the membrane proximal recruitment of each of these signaling molecules is dependent on mechanical forces with the 56 pN NP-TGT sensors showing the highest recruitment, while the 43 pN NP-TGT sensors had a medium level of recruitment and the 12 pN NP-TGT sensors had the lowest level of recruitment (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: Figure 4A shows quantification of pSyk recruitment at different force levels.

claim: The membrane proximal recruitment of pPLCγ2 is dependent on mechanical forces.
source: We found that the membrane proximal recruitment of each of these signaling molecules is dependent on mechanical forces with the 56 pN NP-TGT sensors showing the highest recruitment, while the 43 pN NP-TGT sensors had a medium level of recruitment and the 12 pN NP-TGT sensors had the lowest level of recruitment (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: Figure 4B shows quantification of pPLCγ2 recruitment at different force levels.

claim: The membrane proximal recruitment of pTyr is dependent on mechanical forces.
source: We found that the membrane proximal recruitment of each of these signaling molecules is dependent on mechanical forces with the 56 pN NP-TGT sensors showing the highest recruitment, while the 43 pN NP-TGT sensors had a medium level of recruitment and the 12 pN NP-TGT sensors had the lowest level of recruitment (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: Figure 4C shows quantification of pTyr recruitment at different force levels.

claim: The addition of ICAM-1 dramatically enhances the synaptic accumulation of BCRs.
source: The addition of ICAM-1 dramatically enhanced the synaptic accumulation of the BCRs (Figure 5A), suggesting the increased sensitivity to antigen stimulation in the initiation of B cell activation, consistent with the published studies in both the BCR (Carrasco et al., 2004) and TCR system (Bachmann et al., 1997; Dustin, 2009).
evidence: Figure 5A shows increased BCR accumulation when ICAM-1 is co-tethered with NP-TGT, consistent with cited literature.

claim: The outside-in activation of integrin does not change the patterned dependence on mechanical forces in B cell activation.
source: However, it was clear that the outside-in activation of integrin did not change the fact that B cell activation is dependent on mechanical forces with a similar multi-threshold effect (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows that even with ICAM-1 present, the multi-threshold pattern of force dependence is maintained.

claim: The inactivation of FAK does not eliminate the general patterned dependence on mechanical forces with a multi-threshold effect.
source: We found that the pretreated B cells still maintained the general patterned dependence on mechanical forces with a multi-threshold effect (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5C,D shows that FAK inhibition maintains the multi-threshold pattern but reduces activation at higher force levels.

claim: The high-end (56 pN) and medium-level (43 pN) but not low-end (12 pN) mechanical force threshold is influenced by the inactivation of integrin.
source: However, it was clear that the high-end (56 pN) and medium-level (43 pN) but not low-end (12 pN) mechanical force threshold was more influenced by the inactivation of integrin, suggesting that the breakthroughs of the medium-level and high-end threshold of mechanical forces are partially supported by the inside-out activation of integrin.
evidence: Figure 5C,D shows differential effects of FAK inhibition on different force thresholds.

claim: The inactivation of myosin IIA results in a significant drop in BCR accumulation for the 56 pN NP-TGT sensor only.
source: Unexpectedly, the inactivation of myosin IIA did not dramatically change the dependence on mechanical forces, however we observed a significant drop in the strength of the synaptic accumulation of the BCRs for the high threshold NP-TGT sensor at 56 pN only, and no drop was observed for the medium-level threshold NP-TGT sensor at 43 pN, nor the low threshold NP-TGT sensor at 12 pN (Figure 5E,F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 5E,F shows that myosin IIA inhibition specifically affects the 56 pN response but not 43 pN or 12 pN responses.

claim: The inactivation of dynein does not result in significant changes in BCR accumulations compared to DMSO controls.
source: On the other hand, when inactivating dynein, we did not observe significant changes in the BCR accumulations compared to DMSO controls (Figure 5G,H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 5G,H shows no significant difference in BCR accumulation between dynein inhibitor and DMSO control.

claim: Each of the three NP-TGT sensors (12, 43, or 56 pN) similarly drive activation of memory IgG-BCRs.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a totally different pattern in terms of the dependence on mechanical forces for the activation of memory IgG-BCRs. Each of the three NP-TGT sensors producing mechanical forces at 12, 43, or 56 pN similarly drove the cells to undergo spreading responses and the synaptic accumulation of BCRs or pSyk signaling molecules into the IS (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Figure 6A-D shows no significant difference in IgG-BCR activation across different force levels (12-56 pN).

claim: The activation of memory IgG-BCRs requires either no tension or a mechanical force below 12 pN.
source: This suggested that the activation of memory IgG-BCRs requires either no tension or a mechanical force below the mean rupture force of the lowest-force NP-TGT we used (12 pN).
evidence: Since all force levels from 12-56 pN produce similar activation, the threshold must be below 12 pN.

claim: The activation of memory IgE-BCRs requires either no tension or a mechanical force below 12 pN.
source: Next, we examined the dependence on mechanical forces in terms of the activation of memory IgE-BCRs in Ramos human B cells expressing memory B1-8-IgE-BCRs. Here, we similarly observed that the activation of memory IgE-BCRs require either no tension or a mechanical force below 12 pN (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: Figure 6I,J shows similar activation of IgE-BCR across different force levels (12-56 pN).

claim: The activation of naive B1-8-IgM-BCRs expressed in Ramos B cells is dependent on mechanical force with a multi-threshold effect.
source: As a system control, it was clear that the activation of the naive B1-8-IgM-BCRs expressed in Ramos B cells was also dependent on mechanical force with a multi-threshold effect (Figure 6K,L).
evidence: Figure 6K,L shows force-dependent activation of IgM-BCR in Ramos cells, serving as a control.

claim: J558L cells expressing GGM (IgG with IgM tail) show force-dependent activation similar to naive IgM-BCR.
source: We found that the J558L cells expressing GGM showed the force dependent activation by accumulating more BCRs and pSyk into the IS with the higher mean rupture force NP-TGT molecules, similar to the case of J558L cells expressing naive B1-8-IgM-BCR (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Figure 7B-D shows that replacing the IgG cytoplasmic tail with IgM tail restores force-dependent activation.

claim: J558L cells expressing MMG (IgM with IgG tail) behave similarly to memory IgG-BCR in a force-independent manner.
source: In contrast, it was apparent that the J558L cells expressing MMG behaved similarly to the case of J558L cells expressing memory B1-8-IgG-BCR in a force-independent manner (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: Figure 7E-G shows that replacing the IgM cytoplasmic tail with IgG tail results in force-independent activation.

claim: The lower mechanical force threshold of memory IgG-BCR activation depends on its cytoplasmic tail.
source: All of these results suggested that the lower mechanical force threshold of memory IgG-BCR activation depends on its cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: The tail-swap experiments in Figure 7 demonstrate that the IgG cytoplasmic tail is both necessary and sufficient for low-force activation.

claim: IgM-BCR alone could function as a mechanosensor.
source: Since such a patterned dependence on mechanical force in the initiation of IgM-BCR does not strictly rely on integrin or adhesion molecule, we propose that IgM-BCR alone could function as a mechanosensor.
evidence: The authors propose this based on data showing force-dependent activation persists even when integrin function is modulated.

claim: 12 pN NP-TGT sensor can induce mild but consistent activation of B1-8-naive IgM-BCR.
source: First of all, 12 pN NP-TGT sensor, the one enduring the smallest mechanical force, can induce the mild but consistent activation of B1-8-naive IgM-BCR when was compared to the control TGT without the conjugated NP antigen.
evidence: Figures 2 and 3 show that 12 pN NP-TGT produces significantly more activation than negative control.

claim: Integrin does not get activated under 12 pN or even 16 pN TGTs.
source: In contrast, integrin does not seem to get activated under 12 pN or even 16 pN TGTs (Wang and Ha, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Wang and Ha, 2013.

claim: The breakthrough of the high-end but not the medium-level or low-end mechanical force threshold might be contributed by myosin IIA.
source: All these data drive us to speculate that the breakthrough of the high-end but not the medium-level or low-end mechanical force threshold might be contributed by myosin IIA.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that myosin IIA inhibition specifically affects the 56 pN response.

claim: Dynein does not play an obvious role in the establishment of the barriers of mechanical forces.
source: In contrast, dynein does not seem to play an obvious role in the establishment of the barriers of mechanical forces.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing no significant effect of dynein inhibition on force-dependent activation patterns.

claim: The breakthrough of the high-end and medium-level threshold but not low-end mechanical force barriers might be contributed by the inside-out activation of integrin.
source: We speculate from these data that the breakthrough of the high-end and medium-level threshold but not low-end mechanical force barriers might be contributed by the inside-out activation of integrin.
evidence: This speculation is based on FAK inhibition data showing effects on 56 pN and 43 pN but not 12 pN responses.

claim: Mature naive B cells use IgM-BCRs.
source: Mature naive B cells use IgM-BCRs, while memory B cells mainly use IgG-BCRs along with a small fraction that use IgE-BCRs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Memory B cells mainly use IgG-BCRs along with a small fraction that use IgE-BCRs.
source: Mature naive B cells use IgM-BCRs, while memory B cells mainly use IgG-BCRs along with a small fraction that use IgE-BCRs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: mIgM has only three amino acids in its cytoplasmic tail (KVK).
source: In fact, mIgM has only three-amino acids in its cytoplasmic tail (KVK), while all mIgG subtypes have 28-amino acid cytoplasmic tails, which are extremely conserved across species (Reth, 1989; Tarlinton, 1997; Liu et al., 2010a, 2012b).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citations to Reth, 1989; Tarlinton, 1997; Liu et al., 2010a, 2012b.

claim: All mIgG subtypes have 28-amino acid cytoplasmic tails, which are extremely conserved across species.
source: In fact, mIgM has only three-amino acids in its cytoplasmic tail (KVK), while all mIgG subtypes have 28-amino acid cytoplasmic tails, which are extremely conserved across species (Reth, 1989; Tarlinton, 1997; Liu et al., 2010a, 2012b).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citations to Reth, 1989; Tarlinton, 1997; Liu et al., 2010a, 2012b.

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of mIgG is both necessary and sufficient to confer enhanced activation of IgG-BCR expressing memory B cells compared to IgM-BCR expressing naive B cells.
source: Early mice model studies utilizing biochemical assays and live cell imaging demonstrated that the cytoplasmic tail of mIgG is both necessary and sufficient to confer an enhanced activation of IgG-BCR expressing memory B cells compared to the case of IgM-BCR expressing naive B cells (Kaisho et al., 1997; Martin and Goodnow, 2002; Wakabayashi et al., 2002; Horikawa et al., 2007; Waisman et al., 2007; Engels et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010b, 2012b; Engels et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Syk binds to the phosphorylated ITAM on the cytoplasmic tail of Igα and Igβ.
source: For example, Syk binds to the phosphorylated Immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) on the cytoplasmic tail of Igα and Igβ, and subsequently Syk will undergo auto-phosphorylation at multiple tyrosine sites within its linker regions to be converted to a signaling active form (Saouaf et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saouaf et al., 1994.

claim: Phosphorylated Syk provides docking sites for PLCγ2.
source: The phosphorylated Syk also provides docking sites for PLCγ2 (Weber et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weber et al., 2008.

claim: B cells use different isotypes of BCRs to recognize antigens and initiate transmembrane activation signaling.
source: Fourth, B cells use different isotypes of BCRs to recognize antigens and initiate transmembrane activation signaling (McHeyzer-Williams and McHeyzer-Williams, 2005; Pierce and Liu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McHeyzer-Williams and McHeyzer-Williams, 2005 and Pierce and Liu, 2010.

claim: BCR activation may begin seconds after the recognition of the BCR and the antigen.
source: This is especially challenging since it is known that BCR activation may begin seconds after the recognition of the BCR and the antigen (Pierce and Liu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pierce and Liu, 2010.

claim: After BCR-antigen recognition, B cells immediately begin to spread over the antigen-containing surfaces to form the B cell IS.
source: Numerous early studies showed that after BCR-antigen recognition, B cells immediately begin to spread over the antigen-containing surfaces to form the B cell IS and attempt to acquire the antigens by actively accumulating BCRs and antigens into the B cell IS (Fleire et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2010a, 2010b, 2010c; Seeley-Fallen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The surface density of NP-TGT sensors used in the main experiments is 29.0 molecule/µm².
source: The surface density is 29.0 molecule/µm2, seeing more in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At a density of 4.0 NP-TGT molecule/µm², the same pattern of activation response of IgM-BCRs is observed.
source: At the density of 4.0 NP-TGT molecule/µm2 (5 nM incubation concentration), we can capture the same pattern of the activation response of IgM-BCRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G shows the multi-threshold pattern is maintained at lower density.

claim: At very low density of 0.3 NP-TGT molecule/µm², only 56 pN NP-TGT sensor can very mildly trigger BCR accumulation.
source: At the very low density of 0.3 NP-TGT molecule/µm2 (2 nM incubation concentration), we found that only 56 pN NP-TGT sensor can very mildly trigger the BCR accumulation, while both 12 pN and 43 pN NP-TGT failed to trigger B cell activation (data not shown)
evidence: The authors report this observation though data is not shown.

claim: The low mechanical force threshold for memory IgG-BCR provides an explanation for rapid and high-titered IgG antibody responses upon re-encounter with antigen by memory B cells.
source: All these results provide new explanations for the rapid and high-titered IgG antibody responses upon re-encounter with antigen by memory B cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding IgG-BCR force requirements.

claim: The multi-threshold effect of IgM-BCR activation reflects the multi-threshold progress of delivering mechanical force-induced conformational changes from mIgM to Igα and Igβ heterodimer complex.
source: Here, we tried to interpret our data in a way that such multi-threshold effect of the activation of IgM-BCRs reflects the multi-threshold progress of delivering these mechanical forces induced potential conformational changes from mIgM to Igα and Igβ heterodimer complex.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an interpretation/speculation by the authors.

claim: The multi-threshold effect likely provides a chance for proof-testing of the mechanical forces applied to IgM-BCR during its activation.
source: It is also our speculation that such multi-threshold likely provides a chance for the proof-testing of the mechanical forces applied to IgM-BCR during its activation.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.
